title: Ali's Rope-a-Dope
text:
On 30 October 1974, in Kinshasa, Zaire, Muhammad Ali challenged George Foreman for the world heavyweight title. Foreman was 25, undefeated, and seen as perhaps the hardest puncher in boxing. He had demolished Joe Frazier and Ken Norton, two men who had beaten Ali. Ali was 32, and many observers feared he would be badly hurt.

Ali began aggressively, scoring with quick right-hand leads. Then, from the second round on, he did something that horrified his own corner. He leaned back against the ropes, covered his head with his arms and gloves, and let Foreman punch. The loose ropes absorbed some of the force. Ali blocked, slipped and rode many of the blows, clinched when he could, and kept taunting Foreman in his ear, urging him to hit harder. Foreman, frustrated, threw punch after heavy punch, many landing on Ali's arms and shoulders.

Round by round, in the heat and humidity, Foreman tired. His punches slowed and lost their snap. Late in the eighth round, as Foreman lunged in, Ali came off the ropes with a sudden combination of punches. Foreman spun and fell to the canvas and was counted out.

Ali regained the title he had been stripped of seven years earlier. He later called the tactic the rope-a-dope.
lesson: Against a more powerful opponent, let him spend his strength while you protect yours. Patience under pressure can turn the other side's force into your advantage.
people: Muhammad Ali, George Foreman, Angelo Dundee
location: Kinshasa, Zaire (Democratic Republic of the Congo)
source: Fight film and records; Norman Mailer, The Fight (1975)
caveat: It is unclear how much of the tactic was planned in advance and how much Ali improvised in the ring.
